tagged_preview: <f=6>Read all requirements and instructions carefully. Students must submit the completed form to the student services staff person at the Center they will be attending:</f=6>
<f=16>Obtaining a health clearance is a mandatory requirement for participation and cannot be waived. We must receive</f=16>

<f=17>accurate information about your physical and mental ability to participate in the LIU Study Abroad Program. Information that we receive about you is confidential and will be shared only with those who need to know in order to assist you while you are abroad, including, for example, providing emergency or other necessary health care. </f=17>

<f=20>LIU Global centers are located around the world: Costa Rica, Europe, China, Asia-Pacific Australia, and with international internships in diverse locations, and New York. In addition to classroom instruction, LIU Global students participate in field excursions, community engagement projects, and internships. These field experiences require a certain amount of physical endurance, and the program requires that students possess the physical and mental well-being required to live and study in diverse foreign settings where resources may be different or fewer than those to which they are accustomed. Therefore, students must be able to align their health care needs in these contexts where we cannot guarantee all accommodations. The below is a sample list outlining the types of experiences a student may encounter. </f=20>

<f=22>**Australia****/****Pa****cific****:** Bicycling and walking are the most common modes of transportation in country.​When on field excursions, use of public transportation, some local travel over rough roads, some boat rides, some hiking, standing for long periods, changes of location affecting energy levels, sleep cycles, and digestion. During Fall Semester in particular: activities may include camping, moderate walks and hikes in National Parks up to 5 hours at a time), climbing/bouldering, swimming, kayaking/canoeing, and snorkeling.</f=22>

<f=24>**China**: Use of public transportation. Activities include hiking up and down mountains under altitude of 5,000 feet. Students will visit the edge of the Tibetan Plateau where the altitude is around 10,000 feet -- altitude sickness may occur, but usually is not a concern. **Costa Rica**: Use of public transportation, private buses, walking with inconsistent quality of infrastructure, and boat rides. Activities include hiking in the rainforest on narrow, dirt paths; walking on dirt roads in rural areas; tours of farms; assisting with community projects and leading sporting activities. Tropical climate.</f=24>
<f=26>**Europe:** Use of public transportation, private buses, and walking. Bicycling and walking are the most</f=26>
<f=27>common modes of transportation (uneven pavement – cobblestone streets). There may be stairs to climb in your dormitories and apartments, as older buildings often do not have elevators. </f=27>

<f=29>**Students ****may be cleared**** for participation as long as, in the opinion of the examining provider(s), any health condition the student may have is under control, has been stable for a reasonable period, and has a treatment plan in place for required ongoing care while abroad.**</f=29>

tagged_preview: <f=4>This manual and tool kit was developed to provide individuals with disabilities the information and tools needed to self-direct components of their personal assistance services (PAS). </f=4>
<f=6>Self-direction is a management tool that supports an individual with a disability to oversee and be responsible for the personal assistance services (PAS) they receive.</f=6>

<f=8>Self-direction promotes a participant’s personal choice and control of the delivery of their personal assistance services (PAS). A person with a disability can direct their personal assistant services themselves or they can select someone they trust to direct services on their behalf. Self-directed services means that participants and their representatives, if applicable, have certain decision-making authority regarding their services within the guidelines of a program providing personal assistance services (PAS). When a participant self-directs their services, they take responsibility for the management of their services. </f=8>

<f=9>The law permitting self-direction of personal assistance services was passed by the Kansas legislature in 1989. A copy of the legislation, specifically H.B. 2012 and Kansas statute, K.S.A. 39-7,100, is found in Appendix.</f=9>

<f=11>A Personal Assistant (PA) is someone hired to assist people with disabilities with activities they would do themselves if they did not have a disability. The PA’s job duties are different depending on the needs of the person with a disability. The personal assistant’s job is to assist his or her employer with daily living activities. This includes, but is not limited to, personal care, housekeeping, community access, health, and safety.</f=11>
<f=13>Kansas has three primary models of service delivery. They are:</f=13>

<f=18>With the self-directed services model, the person with a disability is the employer. As the employer there are responsibilities related to managing the services. The individual with a disability is responsible for the following:</f=18>
<f=19>Complete all paperwork related to fiscal management. The WORK program utilizes a fiscal manager to process payroll. </f=19>
<f=21>Advertising, interviewing, checking references, managing, and terminating employment of providers.</f=21>
<f=22>Develop provider duties and tasks so the provider clearly understands their responsibilities.</f=22>
<f=23>Create a schedule for when providers work.</f=23>
<f=24>Have a backup plan in case a provider does not show up for work. The WORK program uses an Emergency Backup Plan to assist with this. </f=24>

<f=26>Some people with disabilities prefer a different model of supports and services. In this model, the individual with a disability is the employer, but has chosen to appoint someone to assist in the responsibilities that come with self-direction. The WORK program allows participants to choose a trusted person to act on their behalf. </f=26>

<f=28>With the agency-direct service model, the agency is the employer and has the responsibility to provide the supports and services needed including conducting background checks. In Kansas, these agencies can include community developmental disability organizations (CDDOs), community service providers (CSPs), centers for independent living (CILs), and home health agencies.</f=28>
<f=29>**Kansas Models of Self-Direction: Supports and Services**</f=29>
